h: A Talking Mummy and a Floor You Can Walk On
p: The building itself is a beauty. The old Mechanics' Institute was designed by Cuthbert Brodrick, the architect behind Leeds Town Hall just across the way, and was built in the 1860s for working people to learn and improve themselves. The museum moved in here in 2008, giving the city's collections a grand new home.

One of the most famous residents is Nesyamun, an Egyptian priest whose mummy has been in Leeds for around two centuries. In 2020 scientists used scans of his vocal tract and a 3D-printed model to recreate a sound of his voice, making headlines around the world. Seeing him in person after hearing that story is a strange and memorable moment.

Downstairs, the central arena has often been used for a giant floor map of Leeds and the surrounding area, and kids love hunting for their own street or school. Look out for what's laid out there during your visit.
Allow one to two hours. Keep an eye on what's happening on Millennium Square, as it hosts events and markets through the year, which can make the area lively.

Leeds Art Gallery and the Henry Moore Institute sit side by side on the Headrow, a few minutes' walk away, so art lovers can easily build a free cultural day. If you've got more time, take a stroll down to Leeds Dock to find the Royal Armouries, home to the national collection of arms and armour.
